subject.name: Sociology
subject.twin_build_note: Path A twin build. Single Supabase row (slug sociology-eduqas) serves both Eduqas (C200QS, England) and WJEC (3200QS, Wales). The two specifications are byte-identical — same content, same named sociologists, same component structure. Use neutral phrasing throughout: 'your exam', 'this paper', 'GCSE Sociology' — never 'Eduqas says...' or 'WJEC requires...'. WJEC alias added to slugMap and boardConfig in index.html post-build (no narration regen needed if prose stays neutral).

article_units.name: Cultural Transmission & Research Methods
article_units.subtitle: Key sociological concepts, the four perspectives, and the research methods used to investigate the social world.

lessons.title: Key Sociological Concepts and the Sociological Approach
lessons.description: Culture, norms, values, roles, status, identity, sanctions and cultural diversity — and what it means to think sociologically.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 'What Is Sociology?' covers the same concept set (norms, values, roles, culture, consensus vs conflict). Reuse 80% of the prose. Add explicit definitions of 'sanctions' and 'cultural diversity' (both named in Eduqas/WJEC 1.1 spec). Keep neutral phrasing — strip any 'AQA' framing. Practice questions and exam tip must be regenerated for Eduqas/WJEC question types.

lessons.title: Socialisation, Identity and Agents of Socialisation
lessons.description: Nature vs nurture, feral children, primary and secondary socialisation, and how family, education, media and peer group pass on culture.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 covers socialisation but lighter on feral children and the named agents-of-socialisation list. Eduqas/WJEC 1.2-1.3 explicitly requires nature/nurture with feral children examples (e.g. Genie, Oxana Malaya — pick one well-documented public-domain case) AND the four agents of socialisation by name. Pull socialisation/identity prose from AQA L1 for the conceptual frame, then add a fresh section on feral children and a four-quadrant agents block. Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: The Four Sociological Perspectives
lessons.description: Functionalism, Marxism, feminism and interactionism — what each perspective says about how society works and where they disagree.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 'The Four Sociological Perspectives' is essentially identical content. Reuse 90%. Add a brief New Right primer at the end — Eduqas/WJEC explicitly names New Right views in family (2.4) and Murray's underclass (5.5), so introducing it here saves repetition later. Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: Types of Data and Research Methods
lessons.description: Primary and secondary data, qualitative and quantitative methods — questionnaires, structured and unstructured interviews, and observation.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L5 covers questionnaires, interviews and observation in identical depth. Merge in the data-types content from AQA L4 (primary/secondary, qualitative/quantitative, official statistics) — Eduqas/WJEC packages these with methods rather than research design. ~80% reusable. Drop AQA's mention of ethnography/case study/longitudinal as standalone — Eduqas/WJEC spec doesn't name them; mention briefly inside observation. Practice fresh.

lessons.title: Sampling, Practical and Ethical Issues
lessons.description: Representative and non-representative sampling techniques, plus the practical and ethical challenges that shape what sociologists can investigate.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L6 covers practical and ethical issues; AQA L4 covers sampling. Combine into one Eduqas/WJEC lesson — the spec packages 4.3 (sampling) + 4.4 (practical) + 4.5 (ethical) as one cluster of three short topics. Reuse ~80% of content from AQA L4 (sampling section only) and AQA L6 (practical+ethical). Tighten — these are short spec topics that don't warrant two lessons. Practice fresh.

lessons.title: Designing Sociological Research and Interpreting Data
lessons.description: How sociologists plan a study from start to finish — choosing an area, setting an aim or hypothesis, running a pilot, analysing results and reading graphs and tables.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L4 'Research Design, Sampling and Types of Data' covers research design — reuse the design portion (~50% of AQA L4). Eduqas/WJEC topic 7 ('Applied Methods of Sociological Enquiry') is structurally separate from topic 4 (Research Methods) and explicitly demands data-interpretation skills (graphs, charts, tables). This is unique to Eduqas/WJEC — AQA folds it into general methods. Add a fresh interpretation block with a worked example of reading a bar chart and a frequency table. Practice questions should include at least one stem-led data-interpretation item.

article_units.name: The Sociology of Families
article_units.subtitle: Family diversity, social change, conjugal roles, sociological theories of the family and the criticisms levelled at family life.

lessons.title: Family Forms and Family Diversity
lessons.description: Nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent, single sex, cohabiting and beanpole families, plus ethnic minority and global family forms.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 covers most of the same family forms but Eduqas/WJEC explicitly names 'beanpole family' (AQA had 'empty nest') and devotes more spec attention to global forms — polygamy, arranged marriages and 'one-child family policy in China' are spec-named. Reuse the UK family-forms taxonomy (~60%) and add a fresh global-forms section with a short box on China's one-child policy as a case study in how state policy shapes family structure. Drop AQA's Rapoports diversity-types content — Eduqas/WJEC places Rapoports in the next lesson (social change), not here.

lessons.title: Social Change and Family Structures
lessons.description: How secularisation, feminism, economic change and immigration have reshaped family diversity. The Rapoports on five types of diversity, plus divorce, cohabitation and singlehood.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 'Family Forms and Family Diversity' includes the Rapoports five-types content. Lift the Rapoports section verbatim (~30% of the source lesson). The rest of this lesson is fresh: Eduqas/WJEC 2.2 explicitly lists the drivers of family-structure change (secularisation, feminism, economic factors, technology, immigration) as a checklist students must address — AQA has these scattered. Build a clean 'driver -> impact' table. Divorce content here is light/contextual; the deep divorce treatment in AQA's L6 is dispersed across 2.2, 2.3 and 2.5 in Eduqas/WJEC.

lessons.title: Social Change and Family Relationships
lessons.description: Conjugal roles, the domestic division of labour, Willmott and Young's symmetrical family, dual career families, child-centred families and the boomerang and sandwich generations.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 'Conjugal Role Relationships' and L4 'Changing Relationships Within Families' both contribute. Willmott and Young, the symmetrical family thesis, joint vs segregated conjugal roles, Oakley's critique — all reuse ~80%. ADD: 'boomerang children' and 'sandwich generation' (both spec-named in Eduqas/WJEC 2.3, not in AQA). Drop the pre-industrial/industrial historical sweep from AQA L4 — Eduqas/WJEC spec is strictly contemporary.

lessons.title: Sociological Theories of the Role of the Family
lessons.description: The conflict vs consensus debate. Parsons on primary socialisation, Zaretsky's Marxist view of family and capitalism, Delphy and Leonard plus Oakley on patriarchal family, and the New Right.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 'Functions of Families' covers Parsons primary socialisation and the functionalist position. Reuse ~70%. Eduqas/WJEC 2.4 is a structured four-perspective walkthrough — and explicitly names Zaretsky (Marxism), Delphy and Leonard PLUS Oakley (Feminism) and New Right. AQA names Zaretsky, Delphy and Leonard in L5 'Criticisms of Families' instead — pull those into here. NEW RIGHT must be present (Eduqas/WJEC names them; AQA only mentions briefly in divorce). Cite Charles Murray's 'underclass' work as the New Right family critique — saves repetition with the stratification unit.

lessons.title: Criticisms of the Family
lessons.description: Loss of traditional functions, isolation, unrealistic expectations, marital breakdown, and the dark side of family life including domestic violence.
section_markers: lack of contact with kinship networks
New Right response to family decline

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L5 'Criticisms of Families' shares the structural frame — loss of functions, marital breakdown, isolation. Reuse ~50%. Eduqas/WJEC 2.5 explicitly demands 'the dark side of family life including domestic violence' — AQA does not foreground this. Add a sensitive, careful section on domestic violence as feminist evidence against the functionalist 'warm bath' view (cite ONS Crime Survey domestic abuse prevalence at the topline level, no graphic detail). Move Zaretsky and Delphy & Leonard out of this lesson (they live in L4 above). Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: Divorce: Causes, Consequences and Theoretical Perspectives
lessons.description: Patterns of divorce in Britain, the impact of legal change, secularisation and the changing status of women, plus consequences for partners, children and the rise of lone parent families.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L6 'Divorce: Patterns, Causes and Consequences' is essentially identical content. Reuse ~85%. Note: divorce is not a standalone topic in Eduqas/WJEC — it's distributed across 2.2, 2.3 and 2.5 — but it earns a dedicated lesson because it's a high-frequency 12-mark question topic and the spec touches it from three angles. Update the 1969 Divorce Reform Act framing to also note the 2022 'no-fault' divorce reform (England & Wales) so Welsh students get current content. Practice questions fresh.

article_units.name: The Sociology of Education
article_units.subtitle: The role and functions of education, processes inside schools, factors affecting achievement and how sociologists research the classroom.

lessons.title: Sociological Theories of the Role of Education
lessons.description: The conflict vs consensus debate. Durkheim and Parsons on the functionalist case for education, Bowles and Gintis on the Marxist correspondence theory, and Becky Francis on patriarchal schools.
section_markers: conflict versus consensus debate on education
education as transmission of norms and values

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 'Roles and Functions of Education' covers Durkheim and Parsons (~50% reusable). Eduqas/WJEC 3.1 is a structured perspective walkthrough — and explicitly names Becky Francis as the feminist theorist on schools (AQA has no equivalent named feminist for education). Bowles and Gintis correspondence theory MUST be introduced here (Eduqas/WJEC 3.1) — AQA puts it in L3. Restructure as a four-perspective grid. Add fresh paragraph on Becky Francis ('Reassessing Gender and Achievement' / boys' laddish behaviour and girls' under-the-radar rebellion).

lessons.title: Processes Inside Schools
lessons.description: Labelling and the self-fulfilling prophecy, streaming and banding, the hidden curriculum, anti-school sub-cultures, teacher expectations. Hargreaves on labelling, Willis on the lads, and Ball on teacher expectations.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L5 'Processes Within Schools' is essentially identical content for streaming, labelling, self-fulfilling prophecy, Willis and Ball. Reuse ~85%. ADD: Hargreaves explicitly named in Eduqas/WJEC 3.2 (AQA has no Hargreaves) — pull in his work on labelling deviant pupils ('Deviance in Classrooms', 1975). PROMINENCE FOR HIDDEN CURRICULUM: 2024 examiner report flagged the hidden curriculum question (5c) as challenging — give it explicit treatment with definition, examples (queueing, hierarchy, punctuality, gender norms in PE), and link to Bowles and Gintis.

lessons.title: Patterns of Educational Achievement
lessons.description: How attainment varies by gender, social class and ethnicity in contemporary Britain. Reading and interpreting attainment-gap data and patterns from official statistics.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L4 'Factors Affecting Educational Achievement' combines patterns + factors in one lesson. Eduqas/WJEC splits these: 3.3 = patterns, 3.4-3.5 = factors. This lesson is patterns ONLY — present the data and the gaps, do NOT explain causes (next lesson). Pull patterns content from AQA L4 (~30% of source). Most content is fresh: a data-driven lesson with charts, tables and 'patterns and trends' framing. This lesson reinforces the data-interpretation skills built in Unit 1 L6 (a deliberate spec connection — Eduqas/WJEC 3.3 is data-heavy where AQA isn't).

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Achievement: Class, Ethnicity and Gender
lessons.description: Material and cultural deprivation, labelling, catchment areas, racism, the curriculum, more employment opportunities for women, the crisis of masculinity. Halsey on class inequalities, Ball on streaming and Willis on counter cultures.
section_markers: Ball on streaming choice and competition

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L4 covers all three factor strands (class, gender, ethnicity), Halsey and Ball are AQA-named too. Reuse ~80% of the factor content. Strip the patterns content (lives in L3 above now). ADD: 'feminisation of schools' and 'crisis of masculinity' are spec-named phrases in Eduqas/WJEC 3.5 — AQA mentions these but Eduqas/WJEC requires them explicitly with definitions. Add a 1-sentence definition of each near the gender section.

lessons.title: Types of School and Educational Provision
lessons.description: Comprehensive, grammar, academy, free school, private and faith schools — and how the type of school affects opportunity and outcomes.
section_markers: Ball on choice and competition between schools

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 'Types of School and Alternative Provision' covers most of the same school types. Reuse ~75%. Drop AQA's home-schooling/de-schooling/Illich content — Eduqas/WJEC spec doesn't name these. Add a brief note on faith schools (relevant for Welsh and English contexts). Tie school choice to Ball's work on marketisation (already covered in L4 — cross-reference). Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: Researching Education
lessons.description: Applying methods to schools — observation in classrooms, interviewing pupils and teachers, analysing exam data, and the practical and ethical challenges of researching young people.
section_markers: official statistics on education as data

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L6 'Researching Education' is a near-perfect match. Reuse ~90%. The spec note in Eduqas/WJEC says research methods should 'permeate the entire course' — this lesson is the explicit application bridge for the education topic. Practice questions fresh in Eduqas/WJEC formats.

article_units.name: Social Differentiation and Stratification
article_units.subtitle: Sociological theories of stratification, power and authority, life chances, equality and inequality, and poverty as a social issue.

lessons.title: Sociological Theories of Stratification
lessons.description: Conflict vs consensus on stratification. Davis and Moore on functional necessity, Marx on the two class system, Weber on class status and party, and feminist views on patriarchy and stratification.
section_markers: conflict versus consensus debate on stratification
theory of class status and party
feminist views on patriarchy and stratification

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 'Functionalist Theory of Stratification' covers Davis and Moore (reuse ~50%). Eduqas/WJEC 5.1 demands all four perspectives in one lesson with Weber treated as a SEPARATE position (not just a Marxist alternative). AQA splits Marx and Weber into a separate lesson (L2). Combine: pull Davis and Moore from AQA L1, then pull Marx and Weber from AQA L2. Tighten the feminism section — Eduqas/WJEC names it but doesn't elaborate. Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: Power and Authority: Weber's Three Types
lessons.description: Power vs authority, formal and informal sources of power, agencies of social control, and Weber's traditional, charismatic and rational-legal authority.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L5 'Power and Authority: Weber' is a near-perfect match. Reuse ~85%. Eduqas/WJEC 5.2 also explicitly demands 'agencies of social control' here — AQA puts that in the crime unit. Add a brief agencies-of-control bridge paragraph and forward-reference the deeper treatment in the crime unit. Examiner-report flag: students confuse authority types (see teaching brief common misconceptions).

lessons.title: Inequality in Contemporary UK: Class, Gender, Ethnicity
lessons.description: Evidence of inequality in income, education, crime, health, family, work and media. The drivers — discrimination, stereotyping, scapegoating, media representation, legislation, moral panics and sub-cultures.
section_markers: equality and inequality in contemporary UK

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L6 'Power Relationships: Walby on Patriarchy' covers Walby and patriarchy (~40% reusable). Eduqas/WJEC 5.3 is a much broader spec topic — it demands EVIDENCE of inequality across SEVEN named domains (income, education, crime, health, family, work, media) PLUS specific named-sociologist treatment of class (Devine on the affluent worker — UNIQUE TO Eduqas/WJEC, AQA only mentions briefly in L3), gender (Walby), ethnicity. This is mostly a fresh build with a domain-by-domain evidence grid. Devine's 'Affluent Worker Revisited' (1992) gets named treatment.

lessons.title: Inequality: Age, Disability, Sexuality and Religion
lessons.description: Ageism, the medical and social models of disability, homophobia, and how religion and belief intersect with inequality.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 'Life Chances' touches age, disability, sexuality and religion in passing but never with the depth Eduqas/WJEC 5.3 demands. Spec explicitly names 'medical and social models of disability' as a binary students must explain — AQA has no equivalent. Spec names 'homophobia' for sexuality (AQA does too but lighter). This is a fresh lesson built from spec. Treat each protected characteristic with: definition, evidence of inequality in contemporary UK, and one named driver (ageism, social vs medical model, homophobia, Islamophobia/antisemitism). Sensitive topic handling — present each as the legitimate sociological subject of debate, not as an opinion piece.

lessons.title: Life Chances and Social Mobility
lessons.description: How class, gender, ethnicity, age, disability, sexuality and religion shape access to life chances and power. Social mobility and the limits of meritocracy.
section_markers: factors influencing access to life chances

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 'Life Chances' overlaps significantly. Reuse ~50%. Eduqas/WJEC 5.4 narrows to 'access to life chances and power' (the power dimension — who gets to make decisions — is more emphasised) and pulls in private schooling and the old boys' network as named class mechanisms. Add a clearer distinction between intergenerational and intragenerational mobility (AQA has these but lightly). Devine the affluent worker is repeated here from L3 — frame here as evidence on mobility, in L3 as evidence of class inequality.

lessons.title: Poverty as a Social Issue
lessons.description: Absolute and relative poverty, material deprivation, the cycle of deprivation, social exclusion and globalisation. Townsend on relative deprivation and Murray on the underclass.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L4 'Poverty as a Social Issue: Townsend and Murray' is a near-perfect match. Reuse ~85%. Eduqas/WJEC 5.5 explicitly names 'cycle of deprivation' (AQA has it but lighter), 'social exclusion and inclusion' (AQA has both), and 'impact of globalisation' on poverty (AQA mentions briefly). Strengthen the globalisation section with a UK-relevant example (e.g. impact of global supply chains on UK manufacturing employment). Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: Walby on Patriarchy and Power Relationships
lessons.description: Walby's six structures of patriarchy, plus how class, ethnicity, age, disability and religion shape power relationships in contemporary Britain.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L6 'Power Relationships: Walby on Patriarchy' is a strong match for Walby content. Reuse ~80%. Eduqas/WJEC structurally puts patriarchy under 5.3 (gender inequality with Walby specifically named) and 5.4 — but Walby's six structures deserve a standalone lesson because they're a 12-mark exam target. Strip the broader 'factors affecting power' material that already lives in L3 above. Tighten to a deep dive on the six structures with one UK-relevant example per structure.

article_units.name: Crime, Deviance and Applied Research
article_units.subtitle: How crime and deviance are socially constructed, theories of offending, sources of crime data, and how sociologists apply research methods to investigate crime.

lessons.title: The Social Construction of Crime and Deviance
lessons.description: Crime vs deviance, historical and cultural variations, and how the same act can be defined differently across time, place and culture.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 'The Social Construction of Crime and Deviance' is a near-perfect match. Reuse ~90%. Eduqas/WJEC 6.1 explicitly names 'historical and cultural variations' as required content (AQA has these but doesn't list them as named items). Foreground three worked variations: historical (homosexuality decriminalised in UK 1967), cultural (alcohol legality varies by jurisdiction), situational (nudity at home vs in public). Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: Social Control: Formal and Informal
lessons.description: Unwritten rules, agencies of informal social control (family, peer group, education, religion, media) and formal social control through the police and courts. Plus sanctions.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L4 'Social Control: Formal and Informal' is a strong match. Reuse ~85%. Eduqas/WJEC 6.2 has a slightly different structure — religion is named as a distinct agency of informal control (AQA mentions but lighter). Heidensohn on female conformity moves to L5 (theories) here, freeing this lesson to be a clean structural treatment. Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: Patterns of Criminal and Deviant Behaviour
lessons.description: How offending varies by social class, ethnicity, age and gender — the patterns that any sociological theory of crime must explain.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L5 'Factors Affecting Criminal Behaviour' combines patterns + theories. Eduqas/WJEC splits these: 6.3 = patterns ONLY, 6.4 = theories. This lesson is patterns ONLY — present the data, NO theoretical explanation. Pull patterns content from AQA L5 (~30% of source lesson). Most of this lesson is fresh: a data-driven walk through ONS / CSEW / police-recorded data on each group. Reinforces the data-interpretation skills from Unit 1 L6.

lessons.title: Functionalist and Subcultural Theories of Crime
lessons.description: Durkheim on the functions of crime, Merton's anomie and strain theory, and Albert Cohen on delinquent sub-cultures.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 'Functionalist and Subcultural Theories: Merton' is a near-perfect match. Reuse ~85%. Eduqas/WJEC 6.4 also explicitly names Albert Cohen and 'delinquent sub-cultures' — AQA has Cohen in L5 alongside the patterns. Pull Cohen forward into this lesson (he belongs with subcultural theory). Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: Marxist, Interactionist and Feminist Theories of Crime
lessons.description: Chambliss on differential law enforcement and white collar crime, Becker on labelling and the deviant career, plus Heidensohn on female conformity and Carlen on women, crime and poverty.
section_markers: female conformity in male dominated society

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 'Interactionist Theory of Crime: Becker and Labelling' covers Becker and labelling (~40% reusable). Combine with feminist theory content from AQA L4 (Heidensohn) and L5 (Carlen). UNIQUE TO Eduqas/WJEC: Chambliss on differential law enforcement is named in 6.4 — AQA has white collar / corporate crime but no Chambliss. Add a fresh ~250-word section on Chambliss using the 'Saints and Roughnecks' study as the canonical example. Also add: chivalry thesis (Eduqas/WJEC names it; AQA has it lightly). Lesson is dense — three perspectives on crime — but justified by spec scope.

lessons.title: Sources of Data on Crime and the Dark Figure
lessons.description: Official statistics, victim surveys, self-report studies, and the dark figure of crime — unreported and unrecorded offending. Police bias, labelling, moral panics and invisible crime.
section_markers: patterns and trends of criminal behaviour
Crime Survey for England and Wales
usefulness of sources of crime data

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L7 'Data on Crime and the Dark Figure' is a near-perfect match. Reuse ~90%. Eduqas/WJEC 6.5 explicitly names 'invisible crime' (e.g. domestic abuse, environmental crime, white collar crime committed at home) — strengthen this section beyond AQA's coverage. Practice questions fresh.

lessons.title: Applied Methods: Designing Sociological Research
lessons.description: How to plan a piece of original sociological research — choosing an area, setting an aim or hypothesis, picking a method, running a pilot, sampling and analysing data.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Cited low: AQA folds 'Applied Methods of Sociological Enquiry' into general research methods (no standalone lesson) — Eduqas/WJEC 7.1 demands a separate, applied treatment. The skill being tested is different: not 'name this method' but 'design a study that would investigate this question'. Reuse only the design framework from AQA L4 (~25%). Most of the lesson is a fresh, scenario-led walkthrough: 'Design a study to investigate why boys underperform in GCSE English in your local area' — work through the seven design stages on the example. The Component 2 paper has been seen to feature an applied methods question worth significant marks.

lessons.title: Applied Methods: Interpreting Data and Crime Research
lessons.description: Reading sociological data — graphs, diagrams, charts and tables. Plus applying methods to investigate crime: official statistics, ethnography, surveys of offenders and the practical and ethical challenges.
section_markers: official crime statistics as data source

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L7 'Researching Stratification, Crime and Inequality' covers crime-research applied methods (~40% reusable). Eduqas/WJEC 7.2 'Interpreting data' is a stand-alone unique requirement — no AQA equivalent. Combine: open with a fresh data-interpretation section (graphs / charts / tables with worked examples in a crime-data context), then move into crime-research application reusing AQA L7 content. Closing lesson of the unit and the qualification — should also serve as a synoptic methods recap.

unique_to_source.lesson: Classical Sociologists: Durkheim, Marx and Weber (L2)
unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: Eduqas/WJEC does not require a standalone biographical/contextual treatment of the three classical sociologists. The named theorists (Durkheim, Marx, Weber) are introduced in context throughout — Durkheim in education (3.1), Marx in stratification (5.1), Weber in stratification (5.1) and authority (5.2). No spec section names 'classical sociologists' as a topic.

unique_to_source.lesson: Education and Capitalism: Bowles and Gintis (L3)
unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: Eduqas/WJEC 3.1 introduces Bowles and Gintis correspondence theory directly within the perspectives lesson rather than giving it a dedicated lesson. Hidden curriculum is explicit content but lives in the processes lesson (3.2). No standalone Bowles and Gintis lesson is needed.

Eduqas/WJEC 6.4 names moral panics and media amplification but does not include a separate 'public debates' lesson on knife crime, sentencing, prisons. The media-amplification content is folded into the interactionist/moral-panics treatment in L5.

unique_to_source.lesson: Social Control: Formal and Informal (Heidensohn placement)
unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: Heidensohn appears in AQA L4 (Social Control). In Eduqas/WJEC she is named in 6.4 (theories) — moved to the theories lesson here. Same content, different structural placement.

unique_to_target.lesson: Designing Sociological Research and Interpreting Data (L6)
unique_to_target.why_no_source_match: Eduqas/WJEC topic 7 'Applied Methods of Sociological Enquiry' is a separate spec strand demanding (a) original research design and (b) data-interpretation skills (graphs, charts, tables). AQA folds research design into general methods and has no equivalent data-interpretation requirement. Fresh lesson required. Foundational skill for both papers in Eduqas/WJEC.

Eduqas/WJEC 3.3 'Patterns of educational achievement' is a separate spec topic from 3.4-3.5 'Factors affecting achievement'. AQA combines both in one lesson. The split allows Eduqas/WJEC to test data-interpretation on attainment patterns as a discrete skill — students need to read tables and charts before they explain causes. Fresh data-driven lesson.

unique_to_target.lesson: Inequality: Age, Disability, Sexuality and Religion (L4)
unique_to_target.why_no_source_match: Eduqas/WJEC 5.3 explicitly names ageism, medical and social models of disability, homophobia, and religion/belief as required content with named driver concepts. AQA touches these in passing within Life Chances (L3) but never with the depth and explicit binary the Eduqas/WJEC spec requires (especially 'medical and social models of disability'). Fresh build.

unique_to_target.lesson: Patterns of Criminal and Deviant Behaviour (L3)
unique_to_target.why_no_source_match: Eduqas/WJEC 6.3 separates patterns from theory (6.4). AQA combines them in L5 'Factors Affecting Criminal Behaviour'. Same rationale as the education split — patterns lesson tests data-interpretation as a discrete skill before students reach explanatory theory.
Eduqas/WJEC 7.1 demands a standalone applied-methods treatment — designing a study end-to-end. AQA has no equivalent named topic. Fresh scenario-led lesson.

unique_to_target.lesson: Applied Methods: Interpreting Data and Crime Research (L8)
unique_to_target.why_no_source_match: Eduqas/WJEC 7.2 'Interpreting data' is unique to this spec. AQA has no equivalent. Fresh lesson combining data-interpretation skills with crime-research application as a closing synoptic treatment.

named_sociologist_deltas.summary: Eduqas/WJEC and AQA name overlapping but not identical lists of sociologists. The deltas below tell content agents which named studies to add or swap when adapting from AQA source content.
shared_with_aqa: Willis (counter school cultures, Learning to Labour)

named_in_eduqas_wjec_only.note: Spec-named in 2.2. AQA L2 Family Forms references the Rapoports — content is reusable, but Eduqas/WJEC content agent must NAME them as the spec requires.
Spec-named in 2.4. AQA names Zaretsky in L5 (Criticisms) — reposition into the perspectives lesson here.
Spec-named in 2.4. AQA names them in L5 — reposition.

named_in_eduqas_wjec_only.concept: Education as transmission of norms and values
named_in_eduqas_wjec_only.note: Spec-named in 3.1. AQA names Durkheim in education L1 — direct match.
Spec-named in 3.1. NOT in AQA spec. Fresh paragraph required — cite her work on gendered classroom interaction and laddish behaviour.
Spec-named in 3.2. NOT in AQA spec. Fresh paragraph required — cite 'Deviance in Classrooms' (1975).
Spec-named in 5.3. AQA mentions Devine briefly in stratification L3 — Eduqas/WJEC requires named treatment. Cite her 1992 restudy of Goldthorpe's 1968 affluent-worker study.

named_in_eduqas_wjec_only.concept: Three types of authority (traditional / charismatic / rational-legal)
named_in_eduqas_wjec_only.note: Spec-named in 5.2. AQA names Weber's authority types in stratification L5 — direct match.

named_in_eduqas_wjec_only.concept: Differential enforcement of the law (Saints and Roughnecks)
named_in_eduqas_wjec_only.note: Spec-named in 6.4. NOT in AQA spec. Fresh paragraph required — cite Saints and Roughnecks (1973) as the canonical Marxist criminological study.

named_in_aqa_only.note: AQA Appendix A names sociological imagination. Eduqas/WJEC does not require — drop from content.

named_sociologist_deltas.implication_for_content_agents: When adapting an AQA source lesson, search-and-add the Eduqas/WJEC-only sociologists named for that lesson before generation. Do NOT remove AQA-named sociologists who happen to also fit Eduqas/WJEC content (Parsons, Marx, etc remain) — only those listed in 'named_in_aqa_only' should be dropped.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat crime and deviance as synonymous. The spec defines them as overlapping but distinct: crime breaks the law; deviance violates social norms (which may or may not be illegal). Some acts are deviant but not criminal (queue-jumping, talking loudly in a library); some are criminal but not seen as widely deviant (minor speeding). Spec section 6.1 explicitly requires students to explain 'social construction of crime and deviance'.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 6.1 — 'social construction of concepts of crime and deviance'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Sociological perspectives confused with each other
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students collapse functionalism and consensus, and Marxism and any conflict view. Each has a precise position: functionalism = society as an integrated whole, institutions perform necessary functions; Marxism = society as class conflict between bourgeoisie and proletariat; feminism = society as patriarchal; interactionism = micro-level meanings, labels and interactions. The spec lists these four and requires students to compare and contrast them on every topic.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, recurring framing 'conflict versus consensus debate' across sections 2.4, 3.1, 5.1, 6.4.

common_misconceptions.topic: Common-sense answers instead of sociological terminology
common_misconceptions.misconception: Examiner reports flag this as the single biggest discriminator between bands. Students write 'rich people don't get caught' instead of 'differential enforcement of the law'; 'girls behave better' instead of 'patriarchal control of women'. Generic synonyms cap an answer below the sociological-terminology mark band even if the substance is correct.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024 (eduqas.co.uk/media/ocvnygux/eduqas-gcse-sociology-final-report-s24-e.pdf) — 'Less successful answers were more commonsense in style and lacked the accurate use of terminology'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Hidden curriculum confused with the formal curriculum
common_misconceptions.misconception: The 2024 Component 1 question 5c on the hidden curriculum was a low-scoring item. Students described what schools teach (subjects on the timetable) instead of the unwritten lessons of obedience, hierarchy, punctuality and gender norms transmitted alongside academic content. The spec names hidden curriculum in 3.2 — students must define it as the implicit, informal lessons, link to Bowles and Gintis correspondence theory, and give concrete examples.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024 (eduqas.co.uk/media/ocvnygux/eduqas-gcse-sociology-final-report-s24-e.pdf) — Component 1 question 5c challenge flagged.

common_misconceptions.topic: Studies attributed to the wrong sociologist
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse the named pairings: Parsons = primary socialisation; Oakley = conventional family; Willmott and Young = symmetrical family; Bowles and Gintis = correspondence principle; Willis = counter school cultures; Becker = labelling; Merton = anomie; Heidensohn = female conformity; Cohen = delinquent subcultures; Carlen = women, crime and poverty; Davis and Moore = functionalist stratification; Townsend = relative deprivation; Murray = underclass; Walby = patriarchy; Chambliss = differential law enforcement; Hargreaves = labelling in classrooms; Becky Francis = patriarchal schools; Devine = affluent worker; Rapoports = five types of diversity; Zaretsky = Marxist family; Delphy and Leonard = patriarchal family.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification — named theorist pairings throughout sections 2-6.

common_misconceptions.topic: Functionalists confused with conservatives on power and inequality
common_misconceptions.misconception: The 2024 examiner report noted: 'Stronger candidates were able to identify that Functionalists accept that there are power differences in society, but that these are inevitable and necessary.' Weaker students assume functionalists deny inequality exists. The Davis and Moore position is that stratification is FUNCTIONAL — necessary, not invisible.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024 (eduqas.co.uk/media/ocvnygux/eduqas-gcse-sociology-final-report-s24-e.pdf) — explicit comment on the functionalist position on power.

common_misconceptions.topic: Official statistics treated as objective truth
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students cite police-recorded crime figures or divorce statistics as definitive. The spec is explicit: official statistics have strengths AND weaknesses (4.1, 6.5). The dark figure of crime (6.5) is the spec's worked example of why official statistics under-represent crime. Always evaluate, don't just cite.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, sections 4.1 (sources of secondary data) and 6.5 (dark figure of crime, usefulness of data).

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'poverty' as one concept. The spec needs the distinction — absolute (lacking resources for basic survival) vs relative (lacking what is normal in a given society). Townsend's relative deprivation (5.5) includes social participation, not just material need.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 5.5 — 'absolute and relative poverty, including the work of Townsend on relative deprivation'.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mis-allocate examples to Weber's three types: traditional = legitimacy from custom (monarchy); charismatic = legitimacy from personal qualities (a magnetic political leader); rational-legal = legitimacy from formal rules and offices (an elected MP, a judge). Students often call any leader 'charismatic' and mis-tag elected officials as 'traditional'.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 5.2 — 'Weberian theory of authority: traditional, charismatic and rational-legal'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Medical and social models of disability collapsed into one
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe disability as a single concept. The spec (5.3) demands the binary: medical model = disability is the impairment in the individual; social model = disability is created by societal barriers. Students must give one example of each (e.g. medical model: a wheelchair user is 'disabled' by their inability to walk; social model: a wheelchair user is 'disabled' by the absence of ramps).
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 5.3 — 'with specific reference to disability: medical and social models of disability'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Methods evaluation reduced to a generic list
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students recite generic strengths and weaknesses of methods without applying them to a specific research context. The spec explicitly demands evaluation IN CONTEXT. A 12-mark methods Evaluate question expects 'why participant observation is risky for studying gangs specifically', not 'observation is time-consuming' in general.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 4.2 — 'value, practical application and strengths and weaknesses of different methods'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Ethical issues treated as a checklist
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students list 'consent, confidentiality, harm' as boxes to tick rather than reasoning about which apply in a given study and how researchers address them. The spec explicitly requires 'strategies used by sociologists to address issues' (4.5) — students must propose practical solutions (anonymisation, debriefing, withdrawal rights), not just name the principle.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 4.5 — 'strategies used by sociologists to address issues'.

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice: Students leave items blank or guess without reading all four options. With 100 marks per paper, a single multiple choice mark is non-trivial. Read every distractor — plausible-sounding wrong answers are deliberately included to catch confusion of named sociologists or perspectives.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Define: Students give an example instead of a definition. A 'Define' question expects a meaning expressed in sociological language — 'patriarchy' is 'a system in which men hold power and women are disadvantaged', not 'when men are in charge of the family'. Each mark usually = one element of the definition.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Identify and Describe: Students identify a feature but fail to describe it. The structure expected is identify (1 mark) plus a developed description (2 marks). Two short sentences score lower than one developed point with sociological vocabulary.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Describe: Students describe one feature when 4 marks usually requires either two developed points or four discrete features. Linking to a named sociologist or concept lifts the answer into the higher mark band.
student_errors_by_question_type.9 marks — Discuss: Students give a one-sided answer or list points without judgement. 2024 examiner report is explicit: 'A common theme on these 9-mark questions is the need to evaluate and analyse.' Top answers present at least two perspectives by name and reach a supported conclusion.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Evaluate: Students recite knowledge without judgement. The 12-mark Evaluate is the most heavily AO3-weighted question. Top-band answers compare and contrast at least two named perspectives, cite at least two named sociologists, weigh evidence on each side, and arrive at a reasoned conclusion. AO3 is 20% of the qualification — students who skip evaluation cap below grade 7.

topic_weighting_notes: Two papers, 100 marks each, 50% of GCSE each. Component 1 = Cultural Transmission + Families + Education + Research Methods. Component 2 = Stratification + Crime & Deviance + Applied Methods of Sociological Enquiry. Equal weighting forces equal revision time. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 2.)

AO weighting is AO1 40%, AO2 40%, AO3 20% — same per component. Students often overweight AO1 (recall) at the expense of AO2 (application) and AO3 (evaluation). The 9-mark and 12-mark extended response questions are where AO3 is awarded — extended-response practice is non-negotiable. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 3.1.)

A minimum of 15% of the available marks in each examination series is awarded for knowledge and understanding in relation to Research Methods. This is a STANDING REQUIREMENT — research methods will appear on every paper, every year. Drill methods in topic context (methods on family research, methods on crime research). (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 3.1.)

Component 2 contains a separate 'Applied Methods of Sociological Enquiry' strand (topic 7) that overlaps with research methods (topic 4) but is assessed differently — the applied strand demands students DESIGN a study and INTERPRET data, not just describe methods. Allocate revision time to scenario-led applied-methods practice, distinct from method-by-method drilling. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 2.2.)

Spec content is set in a UK context except where otherwise stated. UK-relevant examples (Crime Survey for England and Wales, ONS divorce statistics, UK education policy) are expected. Global examples are appropriate where the spec invites them — family forms (2.1, including 'one-child family policy in China', polygamy, arranged marriage) and 'impact of globalisation' on poverty (5.5). (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 2 'study the content in a UK context except where otherwise stated'.)

Welsh-context note for WJEC variant: while the specifications are byte-identical, WJEC students sit in Wales. UK-wide examples remain valid for both. Where examples are genuinely English-only (English/Welsh divorce reform 2022 timing, Welsh policy on academies/free schools differing from England's), note jurisdictional scope explicitly without making it a board-specific statement. Lessons stay neutrally phrased.
current_spec_changes: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology has been taught from September 2017, first awarded 2019, and has been in steady state since. Current published version is Version 2 January 2019. No spec content changes are scheduled for 2026 exams. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification cover page.)

Examination timetable for Summer 2026 is published by WJEC; the qualification is linear (all assessment at the end of the course, in the same series). (Source: WJEC and Eduqas Summer 2026 examination timetable, wjec.co.uk/media/ovdbnkhj/summer-2026-wales-and-eduqas-gcse-october-2025.pdf.)
The qualification is linear and contains no controlled assessment or coursework component. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 4.)

The 2024 examiner report flagged Component 1 question 5c (hidden curriculum) as the lowest-scoring item, with most candidates struggling to define hidden curriculum precisely. Future builds should foreground this concept in the education unit. (Source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024.)
pedagogical_notes: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — disciplinary literacy is critical. Sociology has dense specialist vocabulary. Teach a focused 6-8 term glossary at the start of every lesson and require precise use in extended responses. The 2024 examiner report explicitly flagged that 'less successful answers were more commonsense in style and lacked the accurate use of terminology' — generic synonyms cost marks. (Source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report; Eduqas Examiners' Report Summer 2024.)

EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (effect size +8 months) — explicitly model how to structure a 9-mark Discuss or 12-mark Evaluate response: argument for (cite a perspective and a named study), argument against (cite a contrasting perspective and study), supported judgement. Students do not do this automatically. Use shared-write worked examples before independent practice. (Source: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning Guidance Report.)

Retrieval practice — the named sociologists and their key ideas form a finite list of about 20 pairings. Short, frequent low-stakes retrieval quizzes (study + concept + perspective) outperform single long revision sessions. Each lesson ends with a 5-question knowledge check for this reason. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit.)

Compare-and-contrast as a teaching frame — every spec topic asks students to compare perspectives. Build every lesson around a 4-column perspective grid (functionalist / Marxist / feminist / interactionist or New Right where relevant). Students who internalise the grid have an instant scaffold for any 12-mark Evaluate question. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification — recurring 'conflict versus consensus debate' framing across topics.)

Dual coding — pair every named sociologist with a labelled visual (Bowles and Gintis = school-to-workplace flow diagram showing the correspondence principle; Walby = the six structures of patriarchy as a hexagon). Pair the visual with a one-sentence verbal summary. Ask students to reproduce both halves from memory. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit.)

Sensitive topic handling — sociology covers contested issues (gender roles, ethnic inequality, family diversity, crime, religion, sexuality, disability). Present each as legitimate disagreement between named perspectives rather than as a single authorial line. Treat New Right, Marxist and feminist views with equal descriptive seriousness. This protects the impartiality required by the spec's debate-and-evaluate brief and supports DfE political-impartiality framework. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 1.1 'critically analyse information and use evidence to make informed arguments'; DfE Political impartiality in schools guidance 2022.)

Application as comprehension — many extended response questions are stem-led, presenting an extract or item that students must respond to. Train students to read the stem TWICE: once for content, once for the perspective hooks the examiner has signalled. Every paragraph in the response should reference the stem at least once. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification — 'reading and responding to extracts which illustrate the different views of sociologists'.)

Data interpretation as a discrete skill — Eduqas/WJEC topic 7.2 explicitly demands students interpret graphs, charts and tables. This is a unique requirement vs other boards. Practise reading data BEFORE moving to causes — present one set of attainment-gap data without explanation, get students to describe the pattern, only then explain. Mirrors the spec separation of patterns (3.3, 6.3) from factors (3.4-3.5, 6.4). (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification sections 7.1, 7.2.)

Examiner-flagged concept: hidden curriculum. 2024 Component 1 5c was the lowest-scoring item — students confused hidden with formal curriculum. Future cohorts must drill the definition (unwritten, implicit lessons of conformity, hierarchy, punctuality, gender norms) and the named link to Bowles and Gintis correspondence theory. (Source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024.)

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: The sociological imagination enables us to grasp history and biography and the relations between the two within society.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: C. Wright Mills

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: Society does not consist of individuals but expresses the sum of interrelations, the relations within which these individuals stand.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Karl Marx

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: The first thing to know about poverty is that it is not the same as inequality.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Peter Townsend

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: We do not see things as they are. We see them as we are.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Anaïs Nin

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: Power is not a means; it is an end.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: George Orwell
